newsitem.title: RUSSIA: AGROKHLEB - Russia winter grain outlook still mixed.
newsitem.headline: AGROKHLEB - Russia winter grain outlook still mixed.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from SovEcon Ltd, an independent research organisation specialising in agricultural production and trade in the former Soviet Union.
MOSCOW, March 20 - SovEcon's forecast for total Russian wheat output in 1997 remains unchanged in a range of 16.0-17.5 million tonnes, from 17.1 million tonnes in 1996.
The forecast for North Caucasus output has been revised up by 0.2 million tonnes to 9.0 million tonnes (7.7 million in 1996), thus offsetting lower output forecast in other regions.
However, some increase in the share of poor plantings, particularly in the Urals -- the second largest rye producing region -- is likely to reduce 1997 rye output.

At this stage of the campaign, forecasts for winter rye output in 1997 have been revised down by 0.2 million tonnes to 4.9 million tonnes -- or in a range of 4.3-5.3 million -- around 16 percent down on last year.
It will be the second lowest rye harvest since the early 1970s after 1995.
Russia is therefore likely to remain a small net importer of rye in 1997/98.
According to the Russian Hydrometeorology Committee's estimates, weather conditions for crop development remain mainly satisfactory in most winter grain producing areas.
But by the beginning of crop vegetation, the share of plantings in poor condition -- a strong indicator of expected winter-kill losses -- has increased in all areas except the North Caucasus.
It particularly concerns the Urals and West Siberia.
However, the share of plantings in poor condition in most regions in 1997 remains close to the 1991/92-1995/96 average.

In the Urals it is significantly higher, while the share of poor plantings in the North Caucasus and Central-Chernozem region (the Black Earth) is abnormally low, particularly in the North Caucasus -- the major winter wheat producer in Russia.
